lessons.title: Reading and drawing conversion graphs
lessons.summary: Read axes and scales, plot data and use a straight graph to convert in either direction.
lessons.objective: Read axes and scales, plot data and use a straight graph to convert in either direction.
lessons.before: Read the label and unit on each axis before looking at the data.
lessons.ideas:
Choose scales that fit all the data. Label both axes with their units. Use a straight line when the quantities are related by a constant scale factor.

Start on the axis that measures the given quantity.

Use differences between two points to work out a rate of change.
lessons.method:
How do I read from the horizontal axis?

Read what both axes measure. Find the given input on the horizontal scale, then go up to the line and across to the other scale.

How do I read in the opposite direction?

If the known value belongs to the vertical axis, start on that axis. Go across to the line, then down.

What if the line does not start at zero?

A cost graph might start at a fixed fee. Its height tells you the total cost and its gradient tells you the extra cost for one unit.
mistakes: Check the value of one small division before reading a position between labels.
A backwards reading uses the same graph. It changes the direction in which you read.
Dividing the total cost by an item count includes the fixed fee.

lessons.title: Distance–time graphs
lessons.summary: Read a distance from home, find stops and work out speed for one segment or an entire journey.
lessons.objective: Read a distance from home, find stops and work out speed for one segment or an entire journey.
lessons.before: Read the label and unit on each axis before looking at the data.
lessons.ideas:
Subtract the starting time of the flat segment from its ending time.

Use the absolute change in distance from home and divide by the elapsed time on that part.

Divide total distance travelled by the total time, including any stops.
lessons.method:
What does a flat segment mean?

Check what the vertical axis measures. When the distance from home stays the same along a flat straight segment, the journey graph describes a stop.

What does a falling distance from home show?

A straight downward segment shows distance from the start decreasing steadily. The traveller is returning towards home.

What distance should I use for a whole journey?

Add the lengths of the parts that were travelled. A trip out and back can start and finish at the same place while still covering a distance.
mistakes: A horizontal line on a speed–time graph means something different.
Speed is non-negative even when the distance-from-home graph has a negative slope.
An average of the segment speeds is valid only when the segment times match.

lessons.title: Steady rates on straight practical graphs
lessons.summary: Use a change triangle to find and compare rates on graphs with units.
lessons.objective: Use a change triangle to find and compare rates on graphs with units.
lessons.before: Read the label and unit on each axis before looking at the data.
lessons.ideas:
Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change.

The starting amount belongs to the total. The rate tells you how much is added over another interval.

The steeper line corresponds to the bigger rate when axes have the same scales.
lessons.method:
Why do the differences matter?

Choose two clear points on the straight segment. Form a change triangle with a horizontal run and vertical rise.

How do I use a rate to predict a change?

When the rate stays constant, each extra hour adds the same amount. Multiply the gradient by the time interval to find the change.

How can I compare two rates fairly?

Work out both rates in matching units. Then compare how much changes in one unit of time or distance.
mistakes: Measure both changes in the units on the axes.
If a question asks for extra volume, keep it separate from the total volume.
Use numbers to compare gradients from diagrams with different scales.

lessons.title: Speed–time graphs (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use gradients for acceleration and areas under a graph for distance travelled.
lessons.objective: Use gradients for acceleration and areas under a graph for distance travelled.
lessons.before: Read the label and unit on each axis before looking at the data.
lessons.ideas:
Divide change in speed in metres per second by change in time in seconds.

For the magnitude of deceleration, give the positive size of the negative gradient.

Add the areas for all the required segments. Metres per second multiplied by seconds gives metres.
lessons.method:
How do I find acceleration from a rising segment?

Vertical change on a speed–time graph is change in speed. Dividing that change by time gives acceleration.

What does a negative gradient describe?

A downward segment shows the speed is falling. The signed change in speed is negative.

Which calculation gives the distance travelled?

Find the area between the speed line and the horizontal axis. Split a piecewise straight graph into rectangles and triangles if that helps.
mistakes: A flat segment at a positive speed means constant motion, not a stop.
The speed itself is still non-negative on a speed–time graph.
A gradient on a speed graph gives an acceleration, not a total distance.

lessons.title: Estimating a rate using a tangent (Extended)
lessons.summary: Place a tangent at the requested point and use its slope as the rate at that point.
lessons.objective: Place a tangent at the requested point and use its slope as the rate at that point.
lessons.before: Read the label and unit on each axis before looking at the data.
lessons.ideas:
Use a wide triangle on the tangent to reduce the effect of small reading errors.

Give a signed gradient for rate of change. Give a positive magnitude when asked how much is lost per unit.

A high graph value can have a shallow slope. Use the tangent for the rate.
lessons.method:
Which line should I use on a curved graph?

Draw a straight line whose direction matches the curve at the requested point. Choose two readable points on the tangent line.

How do I explain a falling tangent?

A tangent falls from left to right when the vertical quantity is decreasing. The gradient carries a minus sign.

How do I describe changes in steepness?

Compare the gradient estimates at the requested points. A larger positive slope means the quantity is growing faster if the axes use the same units.
mistakes: The two points used for the gradient lie on the tangent. They need not lie on the curve.
Read the units before comparing the values.
Keep a sensible level of precision for a gradient you estimate from a graph.

examples.title: Estimate a rate using two tangent points
examples.question: A volume–time curve has a tangent drawn. Two readable points on that same tangent are \((3,14)\) and \((6,23)\). Time is in minutes and volume is in litres. Estimate the filling rate in litres per minute.
examples.solution:
The two points on the tangent differ by 9 L and 3 minutes.

The tangent's gradient is \(3\). This estimates the rate at the point of contact.

The answer is \(3\).

examples.title: Estimate the downward rate
examples.question: At one time the tangent of a temperature–time graph passes through \((4,31)\) and \((8,15)\). Time is in minutes and temperature is in degrees Celsius. Estimate the decrease in temperature per minute.
examples.solution:
The temperature goes down by 16 degrees while time goes up by 4 minutes.

The gradient is negative. The decrease per minute is its positive magnitude, \(4\).

The answer is \(4\).

examples.title: Compare the steepness of two tangents
examples.question: At two points of a filling curve the tangent slopes are 5 and 10 litres per minute. By how much does the greater rate exceed the smaller rate?
examples.solution:
The larger slope belongs to the greater filling rate.

Subtract 5 from 10.

The answer is \(5\).
